passages.t: A disaster to tell the generations
passages.happening:
‘This is the word of the LORD that came to Joel son of Pethuel’ (verse 1). Joel speaks to the elders and to everyone in the land. Has anything like this ever happened in their days, or in their fathers' days (verse 2)? ‘Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation’ (verse 3).

Then he names the disaster. ‘What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten; what the swarming locust has left, the young locust has eaten; and what the young locust has left, the destroying locust has eaten’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Joel's book opens not with a vision or a call but with a catastrophe everyone in Judah has lived through. Because Joel names no king and no event that can be dated, it is not known which locust plague he describes. The setting is clearly Judah, with the temple in Jerusalem working and its priests offering the daily sacrifices. The elders, the senior heads of families who led local communities, are the first people he addresses.

Locust plagues were a recurring disaster across the Near East and North Africa. Desert locusts breed in huge numbers after good rains, then swarm and travel, eating nearly every green thing in their path. Ancient texts from Mesopotamia and Egypt mention them, and they continued into modern times. A severe plague struck the land of Israel in 1915, and observers in Jerusalem left detailed descriptions.

Verse 4 uses four Hebrew words for locusts. Interpreters read them as stages of the insect's growth, from hopping young to winged adult, as different kinds, or as a poet's way of saying wave after wave. Whatever one swarm left, the next ate.
passages.later: The law had warned that a broken covenant would bring locusts: ‘You will sow much seed in the field but harvest little, because the locusts will consume it’ (Deuteronomy 28:38). The locusts of Egypt were also a story to tell children and grandchildren (Exodus 10:2).
passages.asks: Joel tells the people to pass this story down. Ask what hard times in your own life or family are worth telling the next generation, and what you would want them to learn. And ask whether you have let a disaster be only bad luck, or let it make you listen.

passages.happening:
‘Wake up, you drunkards, and weep’ (verse 5), because the sweet wine is gone. A nation has invaded the land, countless, with teeth like a lion's (verse 6). It has stripped the vines and fig trees bare, and the branches have turned white (verse 7). Mourn like a young bride in sackcloth grieving for the husband of her youth (verse 8). ‘Grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD’ (verse 9), and the priests mourn.

The fields are ruined and the land mourns. Grain, new wine and oil have failed (verse 10). The farmers and vinedressers are to wail over the wheat and barley, for the vine, the fig, the pomegranate, the palm and the apple are withered, ‘Surely the joy of mankind has dried up’ (verses 11-12). The priests are to put on sackcloth and spend the night in mourning (verse 13). ‘Consecrate a fast; proclaim a solemn assembly’ (verse 14), and gather everyone at the house of the LORD to cry out to him.
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a call to the whole community to lament, built from one summons after another: hear, wake up, wail, be dismayed, put on sackcloth, consecrate a fast. Each group has lost something of its own: drunkards their wine, farmers their harvest, priests their offerings. The locusts are described as an invading nation with a lion's teeth, which looks ahead to the army of chapter 2. Stripped bark and whitened branches are what such swarms do.

The crops named were the staples of Judah's economy and its table. The temple depended on them too. The law required a grain offering and a drink offering of wine each morning and evening with the regular burnt offering. When the harvest failed, the offerings stopped, and the daily link between God and his people seemed broken.

Mourning meant sackcloth, rough cloth of goat hair, wailing, nights of lament and fasting. A solemn assembly was a holy gathering in which all work stopped and the whole community came before God. The young woman mourning the husband of her youth is a bride whose husband has died before their life together began, one of the bitterest griefs that world knew.
passages.later: The law set out the daily grain and drink offerings with the morning and evening sacrifice (Exodus 29:38-41; Numbers 28:3-8). In another time of disaster the people gathered to fast and pray in the same way (2 Chronicles 20:3-4).
passages.asks: Joel calls every group, from drunkards to priests, to stop and grieve. Ask whether you have let yourself lament what has been lost, or hurried past it. And ask what it would mean for your community to gather and cry out to God together.

passages.t: The Day of the LORD is near
passages.happening:
“Alas for the day! For the Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty” (verse 15). The food has been cut off before their eyes, and joy has gone from the house of God (verse 16). The seeds shrivel under the clods, the barns lie in ruins, the cattle groan, and even the flocks suffer (verses 17-18).

Then the prophet prays. ‘To You, O LORD, I call, for fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field’ (verse 19). Even the wild animals pant for God, because the streams have dried up (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
At verse 15 the lament turns into a warning. Joel sees in the disaster a sign of something greater, the Day of the LORD, the time when God acts decisively. There is a play on words in the Hebrew: destruction, shod, comes from the Almighty, Shaddai.

Drought and fire have followed the locusts. In the last two verses the prophet's own prayer rises, and he hears the wild animals joining it, panting for God as streams dry up. The whole creation is waiting on God.

The chapter does not stop at grief. It calls the people to the temple to cry out, and it sets up the great call to return in chapter 2.
passages.later: Amos warned that the Day of the LORD would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18). A psalm uses Joel's picture of a thirsty animal for a soul longing for God: ‘As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God’ (Psalm 42:1).
passages.hard:
Does Joel mean that every natural disaster is God's punishment?

Joel clearly reads this plague as coming from God and as a warning tied to the Day of the LORD. He stands in the covenant world of Deuteronomy, where crop failure was one of the promised results of unfaithfulness. But he never lists the sins that caused it, and his weight falls on the response it should bring: lament, fasting and turning to God. Elsewhere Scripture resists any simple rule that ties every suffering to a particular sin, as the book of Job shows, and as Jesus said of the man born blind and of those killed when a tower fell. Many interpreters therefore read Joel as teaching that a disaster can be God's summons to a whole community, without claiming the right to say, case by case, why it happened. Others stress that Joel's covenant setting belonged to Israel alone. Either way, the lasting lesson is about the response, not the calculation.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: Joel's answer to disaster is to call on the LORD, and even the animals join him. Ask what you do first when the ground dries up under you. And ask how you can join someone else's lament without explaining their loss to them.
